summary: Return every value that appears twice in an array of length n whose values lie in [1, n], in linear time and constant extra space.
mainInsight: Value v belongs at index v - 1, so the array can store a visited mark for each value in its own sign bit: meeting an already negative slot means the value is a duplicate.
invariant: nums[v - 1] is negative exactly when value v has been seen once; magnitudes are never changed.

approaches.name: Counter or set
approaches.summary: Count values and report those seen twice.
approaches.interviewRelevance: Fine as a first answer, not allowed here.

approaches.name: Sort and compare neighbours
approaches.summary: Sort and report values equal to their predecessor.

approaches.name: Sign marking in place
approaches.summary: Use nums[|x| - 1] < 0 as a visited flag and negate on first sight.

personalSolution.notes: Optimal. You also wrote the counter and sort variants in comments, which is the right way to reason towards it. It mutates nums, so mention that.

commonMistakes: Forgetting abs() when reading a possibly negated value.
Using x instead of x - 1 as the index (IndexError for x = n).
Reporting a duplicate more than once by flipping again.
edgeCases: The duplicate at the boundary values 1 and n.

cards.answer: Use the array itself as a visited set by negating nums[|x| - 1] to mark that value x was seen. Clue: Every value lies in [1, n] for an array of length n and the statement demands linear time with constant extra space, so values can act as indices of an in-place visited marker.
keyPoints: Every value lies in [1, n] for an array of length n and the statement demands linear time with constant extra space, so values can act as indices of an in-place visited marker.
cards.explanation: A value in [1, n] names exactly one index, so the array can be its own hash table; the sign of each entry is a free one-bit marker.

rubric.clue: Every value lies in [1, n] for an array of length n and the statement demands linear time with constant extra space, so values can act as indices of an in-place visited marker.

promptVariants: How can the input array replace a hash set here?
Why does the range [1, n] enable a constant-space solution?
cards.answer: Values 1..n map one-to-one onto indices 0..n-1, so the position v - 1 can record whether v has been seen. Since every value is positive, the sign of nums[v - 1] is an unused bit: negative means v has appeared. The second time a value appears its slot is already negative, which identifies a duplicate.
keyPoints: Value v maps to index v - 1
Sign bit is free because values are positive
cards.explanation: The range constraint plus the positivity of the values is what the trick relies on.

promptVariants: After processing a prefix of the array, what does the sign of nums[v - 1] tell you?
State the invariant of the sign marking.
cards.answer: For every value v, nums[v - 1] is negative exactly when v has appeared at least once in the processed prefix (a value appears at most twice, and a second sighting does not flip the sign back). Reading an entry therefore needs abs() because it may already be a mark.
keyPoints: Negative means seen at least once
cards.explanation: The magnitude keeps the original value, the sign carries the new information.

promptVariants: Why does the code use `abs(x)` when computing the index?
What goes wrong if the index is computed as `x - 1` without abs?
options: x may already have been negated by an earlier iteration
The input is allowed to contain negative numbers as values
abs rounds the index to the nearest valid slot
abs prevents the same slot from being flipped twice in a row
cards.answer: x may already have been negated by an earlier iteration
cards.explanation: When a slot was flipped earlier and later its own value is read as x, x is negative, and x - 1 would index from the end of the list. abs(x) recovers the original value.

incorrectOptionExplanations.The input is allowed to contain negative: The constraints say 1 <= nums[i] <= n, so the input has none.
incorrectOptionExplanations.abs rounds the index to the nearest vali: abs never rounds anything; it just removes the sign.
incorrectOptionExplanations.abs prevents the same slot from being fl: The flip is guarded by the nums[i] < 0 test, not by abs.

promptVariants: Why does the sign trick break if the array may contain 0 or negative numbers?
Which assumption of the sign-marking approach would be violated by non-positive values?
options: The sign bit would no longer be free, and 0 cannot be negated
The values would no longer map to valid indices of the array
The array could no longer be traversed in a single pass
The duplicates would appear more than twice in the array
cards.answer: The sign bit would no longer be free, and 0 cannot be negated
cards.explanation: Marks are negative numbers, so an originally negative entry would look already marked, and 0 stays 0 when negated. The approach needs every value to be positive.

incorrectOptionExplanations.The values would no longer map to valid: This is about the range [1, n], a separate requirement from positivity.
incorrectOptionExplanations.The array could no longer be traversed i: The pass count is unrelated to the sign of the values.
incorrectOptionExplanations.The duplicates would appear more than tw: The number of repeats is bounded by the statement, not by the sign.

promptVariants: The algorithm negates entries of nums. What side effect does that have and how would you undo it?
What would you do if the caller needs the original array back?
cards.answer: It leaves the input mutated with negative entries. If the original is needed, run a final pass setting nums[i] = abs(nums[i]) (linear time, constant space) before returning, or say that you modify the input and ask whether that is allowed.
keyPoints: Restore with abs in a final pass
cards.explanation: Stating the mutation proactively is a good interview habit.

promptVariants: What is the time complexity of the canonical code?
Derive the running time from canonicalCode.
options: O(n + k log k) for k duplicates
cards.explanation: A single pass with constant work per element: one index computation, one comparison and at most one negation.

incorrectOptionExplanations.O(n log n): That is the sorting approach; the marking approach never sorts.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(n^2): No element is compared against all the others.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(n + k log k) for k duplicates: The duplicates are appended directly, with no sorting step after the pass.

promptVariants: Excluding the output list, the sign-marking approach uses O(___) extra space.
Auxiliary space of canonicalCode, not counting the result: O(___).
cards.explanation: The marks live inside nums itself, so only a few integer variables are added.

promptVariants: Compare the three approaches in your comments: counter, sort and sign marking.
Give time and space of the counter, sort and sign-marking solutions and say when each is acceptable.
cards.answer: Counter or set: O(n) time, O(n) space, no mutation, simplest. Sort and compare neighbours: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space apart from sorting, mutates order. Sign marking: O(n) time, O(1) extra space, mutates signs. Only sign marking meets the statement's linear time and constant space limits.
keyPoints: Sign marking: linear time, constant space
cards.explanation: The statement's constraints select the answer.
